title: La Rocca on Lomax, Souchon, Stearns and the New Orleans press
summary: La Rocca accuses historians and the New Orleans jazz club of lies and press control; Rust says he has checked his letters.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: This is a Negro who had never been recognized, invented by Alan Lomax. With a few jugs of wine and a couple of needles, furnished by the doctors in New Orleans. He was a set up and tell the history of jazz. A Negro who had never been recognized. Saw what the world broke. Nobody ever listened to him, but Alan Lomax happened to be one of the clique. That is Marshall Starnes, I can name him, for I don't have the list of them. They got a whole bunch of them. They live by piracy and lies. That's all they ever did in their life was lie and live on lies. They didn't come to me and find out what I had to say. Any word that I ever said was always wrong and a lie. And they had men to back them up. Tell them that, well certainly you can back anybody up. In New Orleans is a town, all you got to give them is a few highballs and they're with you. You don't believe me going to a bar room and see two men arguing. Buy them a drink and you write down. Well that's the way New Orleans works. And any time a man of education stoops as low as Dr. Sue Sean and Miss Benville have stooped to blacken a man's character. This has never happened since the time of Christ. Now they don't know me. Yet they were willing to print all untruths. This man Sue Sean gave out articles that Tom Brown was a great man. Well the last words of Tom Brown he tells about the jazz club. He said there was just a bunch of fun loving people who went there to play free music and get drinks. They didn't know nothing about jazz. If you don't believe that, you look in my files when I was to take Tom Jim Brown to court. I'm sorry that I had to do that. But they never stopped at one thing. These men that are so great and big today as historians, they will not put their own name behind it. But they get some poor unfortunate musician who wants to see his name in the paper and they put a statement by him. Now do you like control the press? I don't. Those people control the press. If I went down to Times-Pickey and asked them to put an article in for me, they wouldn't do it. But if the other man like Sue Sean, Miss Manville went around there, they're ready to print it. Whether it was true or not. This is the times we're living in. We're not living in times of honesty anymore. We're living in times of racketeers. Rackets in all lines. And anywhere you take up politics is in it. And the first man to bring this down on me was Marshall Steins. Probably other men had written about it. But he is the one over here that went and got the Guggenheimer Foundation. I think I'm repeating myself on that. I'd like you to say something else in there if you can think of anything.

Well, I don't really think I can, Mr. Rocker. I think that I think I've covered everything. After all, I'm one of those people that just like listening to jazz music. I haven't any sort of first-hand knowledge of what really went on. I wasn't around. I wasn't even born when the first records were made, when jazz was created. But I've done the best I can to catch up with it since. And I was determined to come to the second time I came to New Orleans. I was determined to meet you and to see your files and to have a talk with you.
Well, anyway, what I have wrote to you in my letters, you've checked them.
You find that what I have told you. You find that what I have told you. You find that what I have told you.
